entities.summary:
The Progress Party (Fremskrittspartiet), founded in 1973 in Norway, emerged as a prominent right-wing political institution advocating for free-market policies and limited government intervention. Originating from a grassroots movement against the Norwegian welfare state, the party's headquarters located on Karl Johans gate in Oslo symbolizes its ambition to influence national policy. Its significance lies in its representation of a growing right-wing sentiment in Northern Europe, especially during the economic shifts of the late 20th century that favored neoliberal policies.

The party gained traction in the 1980s and 1990s, capitalizing on public discontent with high taxes and state control. In the 1997 parliamentary elections, the Progress Party received 15.3% of the vote, marking a pivotal moment in Norwegian politics as it began to shift the political landscape toward more conservative approaches. By 2001, the party entered into a coalition government, showcasing its ability to transition from opposition to governance, thus altering the political dynamics in Norway and influencing policy decisions on immigration, taxation, and social welfare.

The legacy of the Progress Party is evident in its ongoing impact on Norwegian political discourse and the rise of similar right-wing parties across Europe. It has contributed to a broader discussion about nationalism and immigration, particularly in a time when Europe faced significant demographic changes and challenges. The party has also inspired younger generations of politicians who advocate for similar agendas, solidifying its role in shaping contemporary Norwegian society.
